disclaimer: PhyVision estimates body shape from a 2-D silhouette. It does not measure body fat, weight, muscle mass or health, and it is not a medical device. These guides are general fitness education. Talk to a doctor or registered dietitian before starting a new diet or exercise programme, especially if you have a medical condition, are pregnant, are under 18, or are recovering from injury.

skinny.title: Skinny
skinny.tagline: Lean frame with low muscle and body mass
skinny.summary: Your silhouette shows a narrow frame: slim shoulders, a small waist and thin arms and legs. That is a great starting point for building strength. The priority is to add lean muscle with progressive resistance training and to eat enough, consistently, to fuel that growth.
goals: Gain lean muscle mass gradually (a realistic pace is about 0.25 to 0.5 kg per week)
Build full-body strength, especially in the big compound lifts
Eat consistently in a small energy surplus with plenty of protein
Improve sleep and recovery so the training actually turns into muscle

training.focus: Progressive strength training 3 to 4 days a week. Keep cardio light (2 short sessions of walking or cycling) so you are not burning the energy you need for growth.

weekly_plan.session: Full body A: squat, bench press, row, plank
Rest or a 20-minute easy walk
Full body B: deadlift or hip hinge, overhead press, pull-ups or lat pulldown, lunges
Rest and mobility
Full body A (add a little weight or one more rep than Monday)
Optional: light cardio and core work
Full rest

training.progression: Work in the 6 to 12 rep range for 3 sets. When you can do the top of the rep range with good form on every set, add a small amount of weight next session.

nutrition: Eat about 250 to 500 kcal a day above your maintenance needs. If your weight has not moved in two weeks, add a little more.
Aim for roughly 1.6 to 2.2 g of protein per kg of body weight per day, spread across 3 to 5 meals.
Use energy-dense whole foods: nuts and nut butters, whole milk or yoghurt, olive oil, rice, oats, potatoes, eggs, fish and lean meat or tofu and lentils.
Drink calories when appetite is low: a smoothie of milk, banana, oats and peanut butter is an easy 600+ kcal.
Do not skip breakfast and keep snacks within reach. Consistency beats huge single meals.
sample_day: Breakfast: oats cooked in milk with banana, peanut butter and eggs
Snack: Greek yoghurt with granola and nuts
Lunch: rice, chicken or tofu, vegetables and olive oil
Post-workout: smoothie (milk, fruit, oats, nut butter)
Dinner: salmon or lentil curry, potatoes, salad
Evening: cottage cheese or a glass of milk with toast
lifestyle: Sleep 7 to 9 hours. Muscle is built during recovery.
Track body weight weekly (same day, same time) and progress photos monthly.
Limit long, intense cardio sessions while bulking.
Be patient: visible change usually takes 8 to 12 weeks.
cautions: If you are underweight and struggle to eat, lose weight without trying, or feel unwell, see a doctor to rule out medical causes.
If food, eating or body image feel stressful, please talk to a health professional. Support is available.

normal.title: Normal
normal.summary: Your silhouette shows balanced proportions: shoulders, waist and hips are in typical ratios and limb size is average. The goal is to stay healthy and choose a direction, whether that is more strength, better endurance or a leaner, more athletic look.
goals: Maintain a healthy body composition and waist size
Meet the activity guideline of at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week plus 2 strength sessions
Pick a direction: build muscle (recomposition), improve fitness, or both
Build habits that last: sleep, movement and mostly whole foods

training.focus: A balanced mix of strength training (3 days) and cardiovascular work (2 to 3 days), with daily movement such as walking.

weekly_plan.session: Upper body strength: push-ups or bench, rows, shoulder press, curls
Cardio: 30 to 40 minutes brisk walk, jog or bike
Lower body strength: squats, hip hinges, lunges, calf raises, core
Active recovery: yoga or mobility, 8,000+ steps
Full body strength circuit
Intervals: 6 to 10 rounds of 1 minute hard, 2 minutes easy, or a sport you enjoy
Rest or a long easy walk

training.progression: Add a rep, a set or a little load every week or two. Track your cardio (distance, pace or heart rate) to see improvement.

nutrition: Eat around maintenance. To build muscle while staying lean (recomposition), keep protein high and calories close to maintenance.
Aim for about 1.2 to 1.6 g of protein per kg of body weight per day.
Fill half your plate with vegetables and fruit, a quarter with protein and a quarter with whole grains or starchy vegetables.
Keep ultra-processed snacks and sugary drinks occasional rather than daily.
Drink water through the day and around workouts.
sample_day: Breakfast: wholegrain toast, eggs, fruit
Lunch: quinoa or rice bowl with beans or chicken and vegetables
Snack: fruit and a handful of nuts
Dinner: fish, tofu or lean meat with roasted vegetables and potatoes
Optional: yoghurt or a protein shake after training
lifestyle: Break up long periods of sitting every hour.
Measure your waist every month. It tracks health better than the scale alone.
Manage stress with walks, hobbies and social time.
cautions: Increase training volume gradually (about 10% per week) to avoid overuse injuries.
Warm up before hard sessions and get pain checked if it does not settle.

athletic.title: Athletic
athletic.tagline: Muscular build with a strong shoulder-to-waist taper
athletic.summary: Your silhouette shows broad shoulders relative to the waist and well-developed arms and legs, the classic V-taper of a trained body. The focus now is smart programming: keep progressing without burning out, balance strength with mobility and conditioning, and protect your joints.
goals: Keep making progress with structured, periodised training
Balance strength with mobility, conditioning and injury prevention
Maintain healthy body composition year-round, not just for a peak

training.focus: 4 to 5 structured sessions a week (for example an upper/lower or push/pull/legs split), 1 to 2 conditioning sessions, and regular deload weeks.

weekly_plan.session: Upper strength: heavy press and pull, 4 to 6 reps
Lower strength: squat, deadlift variation, single-leg work
Conditioning and mobility: zone-2 cardio 30 to 45 minutes plus hips, thoracic spine and shoulders
Upper hypertrophy: 8 to 15 reps, more volume
Lower hypertrophy and posterior chain
Sport, sprints or intervals
Rest

training.progression: Run 3 to 5 week blocks of rising intensity followed by a lighter deload week. Log your lifts and adjust when the bar speed or sleep drops.

nutrition: Eat to your goal: maintenance to stay where you are, a small surplus (about 200 to 300 kcal) to keep gaining muscle, a small deficit to lean out.
Protein about 1.6 to 2.2 g per kg of body weight per day, including 20 to 40 g around training.
Carbohydrates fuel hard training. Put most of them around your sessions.
Include omega-3 sources (oily fish, walnuts, flax), fruit and vegetables for recovery.
Hydrate well, and replace sodium if you sweat heavily.
sample_day: Breakfast: eggs or tofu scramble, oats, berries
Pre-workout: banana and yoghurt
Post-workout: rice, lean protein, vegetables
Snack: protein shake or cottage cheese with fruit
Dinner: salmon or beans, sweet potato, greens
lifestyle: Sleep 8 hours or more during heavy training blocks.
Schedule a deload every 4 to 6 weeks.
Do 10 minutes of mobility work most days.
Watch for overtraining signs: poor sleep, persistent soreness, falling performance, low mood.
cautions: Avoid supplements or substances that are not third-party tested. Anabolic steroids carry serious health risks.
Get persistent joint pain assessed rather than training through it.

obese.title: Obese
obese.tagline: Higher body-mass silhouette, wider at the waist
obese.summary: Your silhouette is wider through the waist and middle than through the shoulders, which usually indicates a higher level of body fat. That is common and very changeable. Small, steady changes in movement, food and sleep make a real difference to health, often well before the scale moves much. You deserve a plan that is kind and sustainable.
goals: Improve health markers such as blood pressure, blood sugar, fitness and mobility
Reduce waist size and body fat gradually and safely (about 0.5 to 1% of body weight per week)
Build daily movement and strength so everyday tasks feel easier
Create eating habits you can keep for life rather than a short crash diet

training.focus: Start where you are with low-impact activity and simple strength work. Build up to at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week plus 2 to 3 strength sessions.

weekly_plan.session: Walk 20 to 30 minutes at a comfortable pace, plus a 15-minute strength circuit (sit-to-stand, wall push-ups, band rows)
Low-impact cardio: cycling, swimming, water aerobics or an elliptical, 20 to 30 minutes
Walk, plus gentle mobility and balance work
Strength circuit (same as Monday, try one more round or rep)
Low-impact cardio 25 to 35 minutes
A longer walk outdoors, a hike or an active hobby
Rest and stretching

training.progression: Add 5 minutes of walking or about 1,000 daily steps each week. Once circuits feel easy, add a round, light dumbbells or a slightly higher step.

nutrition: Aim for a moderate energy deficit (often around 500 kcal a day below maintenance). Avoid very low-calorie crash diets unless medically supervised.
Build meals around protein (about 1.2 to 1.6 g per kg of goal body weight) and vegetables. Both help you feel full.
Swap sugary drinks and juice for water, sparkling water or unsweetened tea or coffee. This alone can make a big difference.
Choose high-fibre foods: beans, lentils, whole grains, fruit and vegetables.
Use smaller plates, eat slowly and plan meals ahead to reduce impulse eating.
Keep a simple food log for a couple of weeks to understand your patterns, without judging yourself.
sample_day: Breakfast: Greek yoghurt with berries and oats, or eggs and wholegrain toast
Lunch: big salad or vegetable soup with beans, chicken or tofu
Snack: an apple and a small handful of nuts
Dinner: half a plate of vegetables, grilled fish or lentils, a fist-sized portion of rice or potatoes
Drinks: water and unsweetened tea or coffee
lifestyle: Sleep 7 to 9 hours. Poor sleep increases appetite.
Find ways to manage stress that are not food-based: walking, talking to a friend, hobbies.
Measure your waist monthly and celebrate non-scale wins: energy, sleep, stairs, clothes fit.
Find support: a walking buddy, a group class or a coach.
Expect plateaus. They are normal, not failure.
cautions: See a doctor before starting, especially if you have heart, joint, blood-pressure or blood-sugar conditions, or take medication.
Stop and get medical help if you have chest pain, severe breathlessness or dizziness during exercise.
A doctor can also discuss further options, such as referral to a dietitian, supervised programmes or medication, where appropriate.
